newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: NGOs in Geneva call for an end to Sri Lanka war.
newsitem.headline: NGOs in Geneva call for an end to Sri Lanka war.

text.p: A group of non-governmental organisations has asked the U.N. Commission on Human Rights to pressure Sri Lanka to end an ethnic war and withdraw its forces from the country's north and east where Tamil rebels are fighting for a homeland.

Fifty-three NGOs said in a joint statement issued in Geneva and received in Colombo on Friday that the civilian Tamil population continued to be a target of military operations, including aerial bombardment by Sri Lankan forces. It also said that extrajudicial killings, rape, disappearances and torture by troops were common.

The statement named some of the organisations as the International Commission of Jurists, the World Council of Churches, the International Federation of Journalists and the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for Human Rights. None of the groups appeared to be from Sri Lanka itself.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) are fighting a 13-year-old war against government troops for an independent homeland in Sri Lanka's north and east.

The NGO statement asked the commission to "call upon the two parties to find a political solution to the conflict which recognises the right of the Tamil people to determine their political status and the need to assure full human rights of all persons in Sri Lanka".
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE says the number is higher.
Bernard Goonetillake, leader of the Sri Lankan delegation to the Commission's session, said in a speech his government had condemned rights violations and brought the guilty to book.

He said Sri Lanka had set up an independent human rights commission to look into reports of violations and that a new constitution, currently in the works, would give additional fundamental rights to the people.
"The existing guarantees and safeguards on fundamental freedoms and human rights have been further strengthened in the proposed constitutional changes," he said.

The NGOs said that the north and east of the island were still under an economic embargo in violation of humanitarian laws and that the government was controlling supply of food and medicines to the region.
Goonetillake said that food and other essential items like drugs were being shipped to northern Jaffna and hospitals, stripped bare by the LTTE, were now functioning.
Food and medicines were also reaching the Wanni region, where the LTTE has moved since it lost its northern Jaffna stronghold to the military last year.

"It has to be acknowledged, even by our worst critics, that Sri Lanka remains unique as a country that provides humanitarian assistance at government cost to areas where an armed group waging a terrorist campaign against a democratically elected government is entrenched," Goonetillake said.
Several thousand people have been displaced during the army's offensive to capture Jaffna and a key highway linking Vavuniya in the north and Mannar on the western coast.
"There are more than 825,000 displaced Tamil civilians living under appalling conditions which include acute shortage of water, food and medicines," the NGOs' statement said.
The military said earlier this week that about 60,000 refugees have crossed over to government-controlled Vavuniya since last October from rebel-held areas and a further 800 come in everyday.
